readerTitle: The clause that mattered more than the price: Microsoft's DOS deal with IBM
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Microsoft, IBM, Seattle Computer Products, Compaq) + 가상 적용 (포장재 제조사와 식료품 체인)
insight: 파트너십 계약에서는 이번 거래 금액보다, 이 거래 밖에서 누가 무엇을 팔 권리를 갖는지가 더 큰 가치를 결정할 수 있다.
misconception: 큰 파트너와의 첫 계약은 받을 수 있는 금액을 최대로 키우는 것이 최선이다.

sources.text: Paul Allen, Idea Man (2011), IBM 계약과 86-DOS 인수 과정
Microsoft 공식 연혁 및 IBM 아카이브: IBM Personal Computer (1981년 8월 출시)
Tim Paterson의 86-DOS 개발 및 Seattle Computer Products 매각 관련 회고
Compaq Portable과 IBM 호환 PC 시장 형성에 관한 일반 기술사 자료 (예: Computer History Museum)

factChecks.note: Microsoft가 Seattle Computer Products로부터 86-DOS(QDOS) 권리를 사들였다는 점은 널리 기록됨. 인수 금액은 자료마다 다르므로(약 5만~7.5만 달러로 알려짐) 카드에는 금액을 쓰지 않았습니다.
IBM 계약이 Microsoft에 다른 제조사에게도 DOS를 라이선스할 권리를 남겼다는 점, IBM이 사본당 로열티가 아닌 고정 금액 위주로 지불했다는 점은 널리 알려져 있으나 계약 원문 세부는 공개 자료로 확인하기 어렵습니다. 카드에는 'widely reported'로 표현했습니다.
IBM PC 출시일 1981년 8월, 약 1년의 개발 기간, 외부 부품을 쓴 개방형 구조는 IBM 공식 역사 자료로 게시 전에 확인하세요.
Compaq의 첫 호환 PC는 1982년 발표, 1983년 출하. 카드에는 'in the early 1980s'로만 적었습니다.
이후 IBM과 Microsoft가 OS/2 공동 개발 후 1990년 전후 결별한 내용은 7번 카드에서 일반적으로만 언급했습니다.

cards.title: The clause that mattered more than the price
body: In 1980, IBM, then the giant of computing, asked a small software company called Microsoft for an operating system for its first personal computer.
The fee wasn't what made Microsoft. One clause about who else it could sell to did.

image.label: A tiny figure and a giant shaking hands over a contract
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 거대한 정장 차림 손과 작은 사람이 계약서 위에서 악수. 계약서의 한 줄만 형광펜으로 강조됨. 실제 IBM, Microsoft 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A giant wants your software.
body: You run a small software firm. The biggest company in your industry wants your operating system for a new machine. Saying yes could make your name.
Which deal do you push for?

options.text: Sell it outright with exclusive rights, for the biggest check you can get
options.feedback: You get cash and certainty now. You give up every future sale outside this one customer.

options.text: License it to them, keep the right to sell it to others, and accept a modest fee
options.feedback: You leave money on the table today but keep the upside if the market grows. This is roughly what Microsoft did.

options.text: Demand a large royalty on every machine they sell
options.feedback: It ties your income to their success, but a hard push could lose the deal. And it still bets everything on one customer.

cards.title: Microsoft licensed, and kept the door open.
body: Microsoft didn't have an operating system ready. It bought the rights to one, 86-DOS, from a small Seattle firm, Seattle Computer Products, and adapted it for IBM.

IBM shipped it as PC DOS with the IBM PC in August 1981. As is widely reported, IBM paid mainly a fixed fee, not a royalty per copy, and the deal **did not stop Microsoft from licensing DOS to other computer makers**.

cards.title: Then the copies arrived.
body: IBM built its PC fast, mostly from parts anyone could buy. In the early 1980s, Compaq and many others built machines that ran the same software.
Each of those makers needed an operating system. Microsoft sold them MS-DOS. IBM's hardware could be copied. The one shared piece in every machine was software IBM didn't control.

image.label: One software box connected to many different computers
image.brief: 가운데 소프트웨어 상자 하나에서 선이 뻗어 나가 모양과 색이 다른 컴퓨터 여러 대에 연결됨. 한 대만 크고 나머지는 점점 늘어나는 느낌. 실제 브랜드명과 로고 없음.

cards.title: Retained rights
body: **Retained rights** are what each side keeps outside the deal: the right to sell to others, to reuse the work, to enter new markets.

The price covers this one deal. Retained rights decide who captures value if the market turns out bigger than either side expected. Microsoft took a modest fee and kept the right that grew with every clone.

image.label: Two scales: today's fee versus future rights
image.brief: 저울 두 개. 왼쪽은 'Fee today' 동전 더미, 오른쪽은 'Rights outside the deal' 열쇠 하나. 시간이 갈수록 열쇠 쪽이 무거워지는 3단 변화.

cards.title: IBM's choice made sense at the time.
body: IBM wanted to reach the market quickly, and it built the PC in about a year. Licensing software rather than writing it saved time. Its leaders expected the value to sit in the machine and the IBM name.
The bigger partner often optimizes for speed and cost on this deal. The smaller partner can win by caring about what happens after it.

cards.title: Retained rights are only worth what the market becomes.
body: Microsoft's rights paid off because IBM's machine set a standard others copied. If the PC had flopped, a bigger fee would have looked smarter.

Pushing to keep too much can also kill the deal, or sour the relationship. IBM and Microsoft later worked together on another system, OS/2, then split around 1990. And hindsight makes this deal look more obvious than it was.

cards.title: Now it's a packaging factory.
body: Your small factory designed an insulated shipping box for a national grocery chain's home delivery. It works well. The chain offers a large one-time payment to own the design.

options.text: Take the payment. A big customer's check is a sure thing
options.feedback: Safe cash now. But if meal kits, pharmacies and florists want the box, the chain owns that market, not you.

options.text: License it to the chain, give them grocery-only exclusivity for two years, and keep the right to sell elsewhere
options.feedback: The chain gets an edge where it competes, and you keep the upside in every other industry. A modest fee is the trade.

options.text: Refuse any exclusivity and offer the box to everyone at once
options.feedback: You keep all your rights, but you may lose the anchor customer whose order proves the box works.

cards.title: Negotiate the rights, not just the price.
body: In a partnership, ask what each side can do outside the deal. If the market grows, that clause can be worth more than the fee.
**Try it today:** pick one partner contract. Write down who owns the work and who can sell it to others. Would you sign it again knowing the market might triple?
